label: Postmodern Relativism / Social Constructionism
summary: Defined by Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives': skepticism toward grand legitimating stories (Enlightenment emancipation, science-as-mirror-of-nature). Knowledge claims are analyzed as products of language games, discourses, and power relations (Foucault's power/knowledge); much of social reality — and many categories treated as natural — is socially constructed.
variants: French poststructuralism (Foucault, Derrida, Lyotard) vs American neopragmatism (Rorty) vs sociology-of-knowledge constructionism (Berger & Luckmann — much milder, compatible with realism about nature) vs later applied critical/identity theories; strong-programme relativism about science is the radical wing. Functions as the principal axis-opposite of critical rationalism on objectivity of knowledge and progress.

positions.summary: Anti-foundationalist — rejects justificationism, but equally rejects the fallibilist's objective-truth-seeking: criteria of truth are internal to discourses and communities, legitimated by performativity or power.
No view from nowhere: universal knowledge claims are unmasked as situated and partial.
Neither pole: tradition, revelation, AND universal reason are all unmasked as power-laden; authority is local, contested, and provisional.
The defining position: theories and categories are social constructions; truth is relative to discourses, language games, and what our peers let us say (Rorty).
'Progress' is a Western metanarrative that masks domination and exclusion; history is discontinuity (genealogy), not ascent; emancipatory hopes survive only as local struggles.
Suspicious of technoscience as an instrument of power and surveillance — loosely precautionary, though the posture is critique rather than policy.
Subjects are constituted by discourse, institutions, and power; agency exists as local resistance within structures, not sovereign individual will.
Deflationary about humanist grand narratives of Man; the subject is decentered rather than cosmically important.
Relativist and anti-foundationalist: moral codes are historically contingent constructions — joined, in tension, to a strong practical ethics of anti-domination and difference.
Typically secular but deflationary: 'nature' itself is treated as partly a discursive category; anti-realist or quietist rather than affirmatively naturalist.
Anti-traditional and destabilizing toward inherited categories and canons, without a progress narrative to replace them.
Skeptical of mastery narratives; nature figures mainly as another contested category.
Locally constructed through narrative, identity, community, and aesthetic self-creation (Rorty's private irony); no universal telos.
The community and its discourses constitute subjects; solidarity replaces objectivity (Rorty).
